hook: Follow how a columnist hooks you, grants a point, turns it with doch and slips in a proposal, so you see exactly what they argue.
intro: A newspaper column on constant availability, in five moves: a rhetorical question answered by the one-word sentence „Eben.“; the norm (ständige Erreichbarkeit gilt als selbstverständlich) and its sanction (wer nicht antwortet, gilt als unhöflich); an everyday scene in a café that proves the point; a concession to the obvious objection followed by the turn on „Doch ich frage mich, ob wir dabei nicht etwas Wichtiges verlieren“; and a proposal in the Konjunktiv (Wie wäre es, wenn …?), fenced off from the extreme position the author rejects. The column is the personal cousin of the essay — first person, direct address (Sie), short sentences — and reading one well means knowing what is criticised, how the norm is described, how the author handles objections and what exactly he proposes.
tips[0].title: The column's moves
tips[0].text: Rhetorical question + Eben. (you and I both know) → norm and sanction (gilt als) → example → concession + Doch (the turn) → proposal (Wie wäre es, wenn …?). Most questions map onto one of these moves.
tips[0].check.why: The rhetorical question plus Eben. means 'exactly, you know it too': it sets up the problem the column criticises.
tips[0].visual.moves[0].label: Hook
tips[0].visual.moves[1].label: Concession
tips[0].visual.moves[2].label: The turn
tips[0].visual.moves[3].label: Proposal
tips[1].title: Concession, then the turn
tips[1].text: Das stimmt, zumindest manchmal. Doch … is the classic concession pattern: the author grants part of the objection and then puts his own point after doch / aber. The answer "he rejects it completely" is always wrong for this pattern.
tips[1].check.why: Natürlich … Doch is a concession followed by the turn: the author grants the advantage, then makes his own point.
tips[2].title: Proposal = Konjunktiv; the rejected extreme comes first
tips[2].text: Columnists fence off the extreme ("Ich plädiere nicht dafür …") before they propose the moderate path, usually in the Konjunktiv II (Wie wäre es, wenn …?). Distractors offer the fenced-off extreme.
tips[2].check.why: The extreme (abolishing cars) is fenced off first; the proposal comes in the Konjunktiv after wie wäre es, wenn.
remember[0]: Question – Eben. – gilt als – example – Das stimmt, … Doch – Wie wäre es, wenn …?
remember[1]: Concession + doch never means total rejection; the proposal is the moderate path after the rejected extreme.
exam: Opinion columns are standard reading in the C1 exam — and in every weekend newspaper.
tips[0].check.q: A column opens: 'Wann haben Sie zuletzt einen Brief mit der Hand geschrieben? Eben.' What does 'Eben.' do?
tips[0].check.options[0]: It assumes you both know the answer: a long time ago.
tips[0].check.options[1]: It asks you to write a letter now.
tips[0].check.options[2]: It says the author writes letters often.
tips[0].check.answer: It assumes you both know the answer: a long time ago.
tips[1].check.q: 'Natürlich sind Navis praktisch. Doch wer nur noch dem Gerät folgt, verlernt, sich selbst zu orientieren.' What is the author's view of navigation devices?
tips[1].check.options[0]: Useful, but they cost us a skill
tips[1].check.answer: Useful, but they cost us a skill
tips[2].check.q: 'Ich fordere nicht, das Auto abzuschaffen. Aber wie wäre es, wenn wir kurze Wege wieder zu Fuß gingen?' What does the author propose?
